reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: An autoimmune orbitopathy most often associated with Graves disease, though patients may be hyperthyroid, euthyroid, or hypothyroid at presentation
Cardinal features include eyelid retraction, lid lag on downgaze, proptosis, restrictive strabismus with diplopia, and ocular surface exposure
It follows an active inflammatory phase lasting months to a couple of years, followed by a quiescent fibrotic phase; treatment strategy depends on which phase the patient is in
Smoking strongly worsens the disease and its response to treatment, so cessation is a key intervention
Disease activity and severity are assessed separately, for example using a clinical activity score and grading of soft tissue, proptosis, motility, corneal, and optic nerve findings

Active moderate-to-severe disease is managed with immunosuppression and orbital measures, while stable disease may require rehabilitative surgery in the sequence of orbital decompression, then squint, then eyelid surgery
The most feared complication is dysthyroid optic neuropathy from apical crowding, which threatens sight and needs urgent treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Thyroid eye disease is an autoimmune inflammatory disorder of the orbit linked to Graves disease. Autoantibodies against the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, expressed on orbital fibroblasts, drive activation and differentiation of these cells. The resulting inflammation causes accumulation of glycosaminoglycans, oedema, and enlargement of the extraocular muscles and orbital fat. The expanded orbital contents within a fixed bony cavity produce proptosis, restrictive myopathy, and, when the crowded orbital apex compresses the optic nerve, dysthyroid optic neuropathy. Over time inflammation gives way to fibrosis, leaving fixed muscle restriction and lid changes.
additionalDifferentials: Myasthenia gravis (as a cause of diplopia and lid signs, and a recognised association)
additionalInvestigations: Thyroid function tests and thyroid autoantibodies including TSH-receptor antibodies
Assessment of clinical activity score and disease severity grading
Orbital CT or MRI to assess muscle enlargement and apical crowding
Visual acuity, colour vision, visual fields, and pupillary assessment to detect optic neuropathy
redFlags: Dysthyroid optic neuropathy with reduced acuity, impaired colour vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect, or disc swelling requiring urgent treatment
Corneal exposure or ulceration from severe proptosis and lagophthalmos
Rapidly progressive proptosis or globe subluxation
Marked orbital congestion with raised intraocular pressure
reference.prognosis: Many patients have mild, self-limiting disease, but moderate-to-severe cases can leave lasting proptosis, diplopia, and disfigurement; optic neuropathy risks permanent visual loss if not treated promptly, and smoking cessation improves the overall outlook.
pitfalls: Assuming euthyroid patients cannot have thyroid eye disease and delaying diagnosis
Missing early optic neuropathy because central acuity can be preserved while colour vision and fields deteriorate
Performing rehabilitative surgery during the active inflammatory phase
Neglecting smoking cessation and ocular surface protection
